title: Scientific thinking: gears, balances, collisions, frames, light
hook: A winch's electric motor spins fast but turns weakly, yet the drum it drives lifts a load the motor could never lift on its own. Where does the extra pull come from, and what does it cost?
oneBreath: Scientific thinking means looking at a set-up, predicting what it will do, testing that on the picture, then finding the rule that explains it and using the rule to work the sum on paper. Five corners of physics each have one rule at heart: gear teeth pass one for one, turning effects balance about a pivot, total momentum survives a hit when nothing outside pushes, triangles lock a frame, and light leaves a mirror or a boundary at the angle its rule allows.

ideas.title: Gears
ideas.oneLine: Meshed gears pass teeth one for one, so neighbours turn opposite ways and speed times teeth is the same on both.

ideas.title: Compound gear trains
ideas.oneLine: Because two gears on one shaft turn together, a compound train's overall ratio is its stage ratios multiplied together.

ideas.title: Balancing mobiles
ideas.oneLine: Each bar of a mobile hangs level when clockwise moments, force times distance from the pivot, equal anticlockwise ones, which finds a missing weight.

ideas.title: Collisions
ideas.oneLine: When things collide with no outside push, total momentum, mass times velocity with its direction, stays the same, even when kinetic energy is lost.

ideas.title: Structures
ideas.oneLine: A frame of pinned bars built from triangles cannot fold, and balancing the forces joint by joint shows which bars are pulled and which pushed.

ideas.title: Mirrors
ideas.oneLine: A flat mirror sends light off at the angle it arrives, so its image sits as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

ideas.title: Refraction and prisms
ideas.oneLine: Light bends at the edge of water or glass because it changes speed, and Snell's law, linking the two angles, says by how much.

calibration.q: Three gears sit in a triangle, each meshing with both of the others. You try to turn one by hand. What happens?
options: All three turn, two of them the same way
They jam, and none of them can turn
They turn, but slowly and stiffly
calibration.why: They jam. Meshed gears must turn opposite ways. If the first turns clockwise, the second turns anticlockwise and the third clockwise, but the third also meshes with the first, so both would turn clockwise at one mesh. That cannot happen, so nothing moves, not even slowly.

calibration.q: On a see-saw, a 30 kg child sits 2 m from the middle. A 50 kg adult sits 1 m from the middle on the other side. Which way does it tip?
options: The adult's side goes down, because the adult is heavier
It balances, because the heavier adult sits closer
calibration.why: The child's side goes down. A see-saw tips by weight times distance from the middle, not by weight alone. Weight goes with mass, so compare 30 × 2 = 60 for the child with 50 × 1 = 50 for the adult: the child's turning effect wins.
